From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ethiopian long-distance runner (born 1991)

This article is about a person whose name includes a [patronymic](link_3). The article properly refers to the person by her given name, Almaz, and not as Ayana.

Almaz Ayana

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Almaz_Ayana_Beijing_2015.jpg/250px-Almaz_Ayana_Beijing_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almaz_Ayana_Beijing_2015.jpg)

Almaz at the [2015 World Championships in Athletics](link_4) in [Beijing](link_5)
Personal information
Born(1991-11-21) 21 November 1991 (age 34)

[Wenbera](link_6),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-1)[Benishangul-Gumuz Region](link_7), Ethiopia[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-2)
Height 1.66 m (5 ft 5 in)
Weight 47 kg (104 lb)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-3)
Sport
Country[Ethiopia](link_8)
Sport[Athletics](link_9)
Event[Long-distance running](link_10)
Team[NN Running Team](link_11) (2022–)
Achievements and titles
[Olympic finals](link_12)*   **2016 Rio**
*   5000 m, ![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Bronze_medal_icon.svg/20px-Bronze_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Bronze
*   10,000 m, ![Image 30: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold
World finals*   **2013 Moscow**
*   5000 m, ![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Bronze_medal_icon.svg/20px-Bronze_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Bronze
*   **2015 Beijing**
*   5000 m, ![Image 32: First place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Gold_medal_icon.svg/20px-Gold_medal_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)Gold

**Beatrice Chebet** (born 5 March 2000) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") and world record holder in the [5000 meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"), [10,000 meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), and [road 5k](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run"). She won gold medals in both the 5000 and 10,000 m at the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") and repeated the double at the [2025 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_World_Athletics_Championships "2025 World Athletics Championships"). In the 5000 m, Chebet won the silver medal at the [2022 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships"), and the bronze in [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships "2023 World Athletics Championships"). Chebet is a three-time [World Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "World Athletics Cross Country Championships") champion, having won the junior race in [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and the senior race in [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships") and [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2024 World Athletics Cross Country Championships").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-6) Additionally, Chebet was the 5000 m champion at the [2018 World U20 Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_IAAF_World_U20_Championships "2018 IAAF World U20 Championships"), the [2022 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Commonwealth_Games "2022 Commonwealth Games"), and the [2022 African Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2022 African Championships in Athletics").

Chebet trains in [Londiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londiani "Londiani"), Kericho County.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-U20X-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-8)

## Early life and junior career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beatrice_Chebet&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and junior career")]

Chebet was born on 5 March 2000, the daughter of Francis and Lilian Kirui.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-WAprofile-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-DN-10) While at primary school, she raced in 5000 m events,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-DN-10) and went on to attend Saramek Secondary School, [Londiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Londiani "Londiani"), graduating from there in 2013.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-DN-10) She joined the Lemotit Athletics Club in November 2016.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-DN-10)

In June 2018, at the age of 18, Chebet won the Kenyan Under-20s 5000 metres. A month later at [Tampere 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_IAAF_World_U20_Championships "2018 IAAF World U20 Championships"), she became the first Kenyan woman and the first non-Ethiopian since 2006 to win the 5000 m title at the [World U20 Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "IAAF World Junior Championships in Athletics").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-11)

At the [2019 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), the top three athletes in the women's U20 race – Chebet and the Ethiopian duo of [Alemitu Tariku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alemitu_Tariku "Alemitu Tariku") and [Tsigie Gebreselama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsigie_Gebreselama "Tsigie Gebreselama") – were all awarded the time of 20:50 as they finished together. Tariku was initially announced as the winner, with Gebreselama awarded silver. However, after the photo finish footage was reviewed Chebet received the gold medal.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-12) During the same year, Chebet won the Kenyan U20 National Cross Country Championships.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-U20X-7)

## Senior career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beatrice_Chebet&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Senior career")]

### 2022–2023

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beatrice_Chebet&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2022–2023")]

At the [2022 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships") in [Eugene, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene,_Oregon "Eugene, Oregon"), Chebet claimed a silver medal in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2022 World Athletics Championships – Women's 5000 metres"), with a time of [14:46.75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2022 World Athletics Championships – Women's 5000 metres") behind [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay") in 14:46.29 and ahead of [Dawit Seyaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawit_Seyaum "Dawit Seyaum") (14:47.36).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-13)

On 31 December 2023, at the Cursa dels Nassos in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Chebet set a new women's only [5 kilometre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run") world record of 14:13, which was faster than both the previous women's only world record of 14:29, and the mixed world record of 14:19 set in 2021.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-14)

### 2024

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beatrice_Chebet&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2024")]

At the [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Prefontaine_Classic "2024 Prefontaine Classic") on 25 May, Chebet broke [Letesenbet Gidey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letesenbet_Gidey "Letesenbet Gidey")'s [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") world record of 29:01.03, running a time of 28:54.14 to become the first woman to break the 29 minute barrier.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-15) The race was originally billed as a world record attempt by [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay"). Chebet attached herself to Gudaf throughout the twenty five lap race, but as Gudaf faded from world record pace nearing the end, Chebet surged with three laps to go to catch up with the world record [wavelights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelight "Wavelight") and went on to break the record.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-:0-16)

At the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 5000 metres"), Chebet won an Olympic gold medal in the [women's 5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 5000 metres") on 5 August, finishing with a time of 14:28.56, beating defending champion [Sifan Hassan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sifan_Hassan "Sifan Hassan"), reigning world champion [Faith Kipyegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith_Kipyegon "Faith Kipyegon"), and world record holder [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay") in a highly anticipated race. Chebet stayed in the pack for much of the race, but as Kipyegon made a surge to the front, Chebet followed, out-kicking Kipyegon in the final hundred metres to become the Olympic Champion.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-18) Chebet also won Olympic gold in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's 10,000 metres") on 9 August, finishing in a time of 30:43.25.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-19)

At the [Weltklasse Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse_Z%C3%BCrich "Weltklasse Zürich") meeting on 5 September, Chebet attempted to break the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") world record of 14:00.21 set by [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay") in 2023, perhaps to become the first woman under the 14 minute barrier. However, with pacing only to 2000 metres and the weather conditions proving to be too poor for a record attempt, Chebet was unable to break the world record or her personal best of 14:05.92, but still managed to dip below 14:10 to win the race in a world leading time and a new meeting record of 14:09.52.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-21) On 14 September, Chebet won the 5000 metres at the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Diamond_League "2024 Diamond League")[final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Memorial_Van_Damme "2024 Memorial Van Damme") in Brussels, Belgium, in a time of 14:09.82.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-22) On 31 December, at the Cursa dels Nassos, Chebet broke [Agnes Jebet's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Jebet_Ngetich "Agnes Jebet Ngetich") mixed 5 kilometre world record of 14:13, running 13:54. In setting this record, Chebet became the first woman to break the 14 minute barrier on any surface.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-:1-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-24)

### 2025

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Beatrice_Chebet&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2025")]

On 25 May, at the [Meeting International Mohammed VI d'Athletisme de Rabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Meeting_International_Mohammed_VI_d'Athl%C3%A9tisme_de_Rabat "2025 Meeting International Mohammed VI d'Athlétisme de Rabat"), Chebet ran the second fastest 3000 metres of all time, finishing in 8:11.56. This time falls 5.45 seconds short of [Wang Junxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Junxia "Wang Junxia")'s officially recognized world record of 8:06.11 set in 1993.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-25) Given the [controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Junxia#After_retirement_&_controversy "Wang Junxia") surrounding Junxia's world record, some organizations outside of [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") such as [Track and Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_&_Field_News "Track & Field News") do not recognize it, which would make Chebet's performance the fastest in history.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-26) On 6 June, at the [Golden Gala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Golden_Gala "2025 Golden Gala"), Chebet ran the second fastest 5000 metres of all time, finishing in 14:03.69.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-27) On 5 July, at the [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Prefontaine_Classic "2025 Prefontaine Classic"), with a 61-second final lap, Chebet broke [Gudaf Tsegay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudaf_Tsegay "Gudaf Tsegay")'s 5000 metre world record of 14:00.21, running 13:58.06 to become the first woman to break the 14 minute barrier on the track.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet#cite_note-28)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Usain Bolt beating Tyson Gay and setting a 100 m world record at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics in Berlin

World records in athletics are ratified by World Athletics. Athletics records comprise the best performances in the sports of track and field, road running and racewalking.

Records are kept for all events contested at the Olympic Games and some others. Unofficial records for some other events are kept by track and field statisticians. The only non-metric track distance for which official records are kept is the mile run.

Criteriaedit

The criteria which must be satisfied for ratification of a world record are defined by World Athletics in Part III of the Competition Rules.[1] These criteria also apply to national or other restricted records and also to performances submitted as qualifying marks for eligibility to compete in major events such as the Olympic Games.

The criteria include:

David Rudisha en route to his 800 m world record at the 2012 Summer Olympics
The dimensions of the track and equipment used must conform to standards. In road events, the course must be accurately measured, by a certified measurer.
Except in road events (road running and race walking), the performance must be set in a single-sex race,[2] with the sole exception of the mixed-sex 4 × 400 m relay, introduced by World Athletics in 2017.[3]
All team members in a relay race must be of the same nationality.
Pacemakers are allowed, provided they have not been lapped; lapped athletes must give way.
Drug testing immediately after the performance is now required for ratification of a record. Existing records which predate this requirement are still extant. Athletes who pass the immediate test but are later found to have been using banned substances have their performances invalidated.
In running events up to 200 m in distance and in horizontal jump events, wind assistance is permitted only up to 2.0 m/s. In decathlon or heptathlon, average wind assistance of less than 2.0 m/s is required across all applicable disciplines; and maximum of 4.0 m/s in any one event. As an exception, according to rule 36.2, specific event organizers may choose to ignore wind velocity readings exclusively for their specific event records (e.g. a performance in a 100 m race at a meeting with a wind reading of +2.4 m/s may be considered that specific meeting record, but will not be considered as a world record).[1]
In running events up to 800 m in distance, photo finish fully automatic timing is required.
There is no restriction on altitude; since the thinner atmosphere of higher altitude provides less air resistance, locations such as Mexico City and Sestriere have previously been the sites of records in the sprint and jump events. See effects of high altitude on humans. Records set at high altitude venues are often marked with an "A" though that does not disqualify it as a record. Under those circumstances, a "sea level" best is also tracked by statisticians. Long-distance races run at altitude, with less oxygen available to the athlete, have been shown to be to the athlete's disadvantage.
In road events, the course is not required to be a circuit, but the overall decrease in elevation between the start and finish shall not exceed 1:1000, i.e. 1 m/km.
In road events, the start and finish points of a course, measured along a theoretical straight line between them, shall not be further apart than 50% of the race distance.
See also: Marathon world record progression § Criteria for record eligibility
Bonus paymentsedit

Breaking a world record is an important event for athletics fans, and athletes' personal sponsors and promoters of major meetings such as the Diamond League and its predecessor, the IAAF Golden League, have offered bonuses to athletes breaking a record.

Some middle-distance runners have specialized in acting as pacemakers in longer races, receiving a fee without even finishing the race, and possibly a bonus if a record results. This is a useful occupation for athletes who are capable of running accurately to a specified pace, but not capable of the fastest times to become champions in their own right.

In the pole vault record bonuses create an incentive for an athlete capable of beating a record by a large margin to instead break it by the minimum amount (one centimetre), multiple times, at multiple meetings, in order to accumulate multiple bonuses. This was done by Sergey Bubka and Yelena Isinbayeva in the men's and women's pole vault respectively,[4] and some commentators have complained that neither athlete ever posted as high a mark as they were capable of.[5] Since 2020, Armand Duplantis has been emulating the practice.[6] In most other disciplines, this issue does not arise, since it is practically impossible to deliberately break a record by a small margin.

World recordsedit
Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone being greeted with a "World records are my favorite food" sign at the 2022 World Athletics Championships

World Athletics (then IAAF) commenced the recognition of world records in 1912, and indoor world records after 1987. In 2000, IAAF rule 260.18a (formerly 260.6a) was amended, so that "world records" (as opposed to "indoor world records") can be set in a facility "with or without roof". This rule was not applied retroactively,[7] and has, thus far, only affected the men's and women's pole vault, women's 2000 m and women's triple jump. The women's vault record has been advanced 9 times indoors by three different women, each ratified as a world record. The last record to be set indoors was in 2004. Sergey Bubka's 1993 pole vault world indoor record of 6.15 m was not considered to be a world record, because it was set before the new rule came into effect. Bubka's world record of 6.14 m, set outdoors in 1994, was surpassed by two different men since 2000, initially by Renaud Lavillenie in 2014 with a 6.16 m indoors mark, and most recently by Armand Duplantis in 2026 with a 6.31 m indoors mark.

In 2023, World Athletics decided to introduce the new term 'short track' to replace the previous term 'indoor' to describe events and performances that are set on a 200 m track.[8] For track and combined events, the term "indoor world records" were changed to "short track world records". In some field events, including long jump, triple jump, high jump, pole vault, and shot put, indoor world records were eliminated. These changes came into effect on 1 November 2023.

World best performancesedit

Records in events without World Athletics-ratified world records are typically referred to as world best performances or world bests.

While races over imperial measured distances were very common in the first half of the 20th century, only the mile remains common today due to its historical prominence in track and field: all other imperial measured distance races became increasingly rare, and the IAAF deleted these events from the world record books in 1976.

In November 2019, World Athletics (WA; formerly IAAF) also deleted several long-distance events (track distances of 20,000 metres, 25,000 metres and 30,000 metres[239] and road distances of 15 km, 20 km, 25 km and 30 km) from the world record books.

Some road racing distances and indoor variations of outdoor events fall outside of WA's lists, and records set in uncommon events usually do not adhere to the strict criteria found in WA-ratifiable events: one example is the 150 metres record, which was set by Usain Bolt on a specially-made straight track, while previous performances (such as the Bailey–Johnson 150-metre race) were completed on a traditional circuit which included a partial bend in the track.

The 40-yard dash, a standard acceleration evaluation for American football players, does not fall within the usual criteria of athletics racing events. In most 40-yard dashes, reaction times are not recorded as timing starts only once the player is in motion, and the standards for timing a "football 40" are so lax and inconsistent that a real world record cannot be claimed.

Performances are also hand-timed and calculated to 1/100 of a second, although studies have shown human beings simply cannot react consistently or accurately enough for this to be a valid method, and even those using light beams are timed by the motion of the athlete, removing the normal factor of reaction time; further, football 40-yard dashes are usually run on a turf surface as opposed to an all weather track. All of these factors make track and "football 40" performances essentially impossible to compare.

The world best time for a "football 40" is 4.17 by Deion Sanders, while the extrapolated best for an Olympic-level athlete (including reacting to a starting gun) is 4.24 by Maurice Greene at the 2001 World Championships in Athletics.[240][241] Under conventional football timing on a turf field in 2017, Christian Coleman reportedly ran a 4.12.[242]

Javelin specificationsedit
See also: Javelin redesign

The men's javelin specification was changed with effect from 1986, and the women's from 2000. The purpose was to reduce the number of illegal flat landings, but a side-effect was to reduce the distance travelled. The prior world records in individual men's and women's javelin were invalidated, but the prior records in decathlon and heptathlon were not.[510]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Usain Bolt beating Tyson Gay and setting a 100 m world record at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics in Berlin

World records in athletics are ratified by World Athletics. Athletics records comprise the best performances in the sports of track and field, road running and racewalking.

Records are kept for all events contested at the Olympic Games and some others. Unofficial records for some other events are kept by track and field statisticians. The only non-metric track distance for which official records are kept is the mile run.

Criteriaedit

The criteria which must be satisfied for ratification of a world record are defined by World Athletics in Part III of the Competition Rules.[1] These criteria also apply to national or other restricted records and also to performances submitted as qualifying marks for eligibility to compete in major events such as the Olympic Games.

The criteria include:

David Rudisha en route to his 800 m world record at the 2012 Summer Olympics
The dimensions of the track and equipment used must conform to standards. In road events, the course must be accurately measured, by a certified measurer.
Except in road events (road running and race walking), the performance must be set in a single-sex race,[2] with the sole exception of the mixed-sex 4 × 400 m relay, introduced by World Athletics in 2017.[3]
All team members in a relay race must be of the same nationality.
Pacemakers are allowed, provided they have not been lapped; lapped athletes must give way.
Drug testing immediately after the performance is now required for ratification of a record. Existing records which predate this requirement are still extant. Athletes who pass the immediate test but are later found to have been using banned substances have their performances invalidated.
In running events up to 200 m in distance and in horizontal jump events, wind assistance is permitted only up to 2.0 m/s. In decathlon or heptathlon, average wind assistance of less than 2.0 m/s is required across all applicable disciplines; and maximum of 4.0 m/s in any one event. As an exception, according to rule 36.2, specific event organizers may choose to ignore wind velocity readings exclusively for their specific event records (e.g. a performance in a 100 m race at a meeting with a wind reading of +2.4 m/s may be considered that specific meeting record, but will not be considered as a world record).[1]
In running events up to 800 m in distance, photo finish fully automatic timing is required.
There is no restriction on altitude; since the thinner atmosphere of higher altitude provides less air resistance, locations such as Mexico City and Sestriere have previously been the sites of records in the sprint and jump events. See effects of high altitude on humans. Records set at high altitude venues are often marked with an "A" though that does not disqualify it as a record. Under those circumstances, a "sea level" best is also tracked by statisticians. Long-distance races run at altitude, with less oxygen available to the athlete, have been shown to be to the athlete's disadvantage.
In road events, the course is not required to be a circuit, but the overall decrease in elevation between the start and finish shall not exceed 1:1000, i.e. 1 m/km.
In road events, the start and finish points of a course, measured along a theoretical straight line between them, shall not be further apart than 50% of the race distance.
See also: Marathon world record progression § Criteria for record eligibility
Bonus paymentsedit

Breaking a world record is an important event for athletics fans, and athletes' personal sponsors and promoters of major meetings such as the Diamond League and its predecessor, the IAAF Golden League, have offered bonuses to athletes breaking a record.

Some middle-distance runners have specialized in acting as pacemakers in longer races, receiving a fee without even finishing the race, and possibly a bonus if a record results. This is a useful occupation for athletes who are capable of running accurately to a specified pace, but not capable of the fastest times to become champions in their own right.

In the pole vault record bonuses create an incentive for an athlete capable of beating a record by a large margin to instead break it by the minimum amount (one centimetre), multiple times, at multiple meetings, in order to accumulate multiple bonuses. This was done by Sergey Bubka and Yelena Isinbayeva in the men's and women's pole vault respectively,[4] and some commentators have complained that neither athlete ever posted as high a mark as they were capable of.[5] Since 2020, Armand Duplantis has been emulating the practice.[6] In most other disciplines, this issue does not arise, since it is practically impossible to deliberately break a record by a small margin.

World recordsedit
Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone being greeted with a "World records are my favorite food" sign at the 2022 World Athletics Championships

World Athletics (then IAAF) commenced the recognition of world records in 1912, and indoor world records after 1987. In 2000, IAAF rule 260.18a (formerly 260.6a) was amended, so that "world records" (as opposed to "indoor world records") can be set in a facility "with or without roof". This rule was not applied retroactively,[7] and has, thus far, only affected the men's and women's pole vault, women's 2000 m and women's triple jump. The women's vault record has been advanced 9 times indoors by three different women, each ratified as a world record. The last record to be set indoors was in 2004. Sergey Bubka's 1993 pole vault world indoor record of 6.15 m was not considered to be a world record, because it was set before the new rule came into effect. Bubka's world record of 6.14 m, set outdoors in 1994, was surpassed by two different men since 2000, initially by Renaud Lavillenie in 2014 with a 6.16 m indoors mark, and most recently by Armand Duplantis in 2026 with a 6.31 m indoors mark.

In 2023, World Athletics decided to introduce the new term 'short track' to replace the previous term 'indoor' to describe events and performances that are set on a 200 m track.[8] For track and combined events, the term "indoor world records" were changed to "short track world records". In some field events, including long jump, triple jump, high jump, pole vault, and shot put, indoor world records were eliminated. These changes came into effect on 1 November 2023.

**Kenenisa Bekele Beyecha**[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-4) ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Qananiisaa baqqalaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ቀነኒሳ በቀለ; born 13 June 1982) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He was the world record holder in both the [5,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and [10,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10000_metres "10000 metres") from 2004 until 2020. He won the gold medal in both the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres") and [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") events at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics"). At the [2004 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), he won the gold medal in the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") and the silver medal in the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres").

He is the most successful runner in the history of the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), with six long (12 km) course and five short (4 km) course titles. He won the 10,000 m title at the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Championships_in_Athletics "World Championships in Athletics") in 2003, 2005, 2007 and 2009 (matching [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")'s four in a row win streak). Kenenisa was unbeaten over 10,000 m from his debut in 2003 until 2011, when he failed to finish at the World Championships final.

At the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") he became the first man to win both 5000 m and 10,000 m title at the same championships. Over 5000 m he has also won an Olympic silver (2004), World Championship bronze (2003), two [African Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Championships_in_Athletics "African Championships in Athletics") titles and one [All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Africa_Games "All-Africa Games") gold medal. He also won the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") title at the [2006 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships").

On 6 April 2014, he produced the sixth fastest marathon debut ever on a record-eligible course with his victory at the [Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon "Paris Marathon"), in a course record time of 2:05:04. On 25 September 2016, Kenenisa won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03, a new personal best, then the third-fastest marathon of all time. On 29 September 2019, he again won the Berlin Marathon in a time of 2:01:41, two seconds slower than [the then world record of 2:01:39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") in the 2018 Berlin Marathon.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-5) Considering his accomplishments in cross country, track, and road racing, many consider him to be the greatest distance runner of all time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-8)

Kenenisa Bekele was born in 1982 in [Bekoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekoji "Bekoji") in the [Arsi Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsi_Zone "Arsi Zone") of [Oromia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromia "Oromia") Region, the same town as several other prominent long-distance runners, including the Dibaba's Daughters ([Ejegayehu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejegayehu_Dibaba "Ejegayehu Dibaba"), [Tirunesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba") and [Genzebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba")) and their cousin [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-9) Kenenisa was born the second child to parents who made a living as [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley") farmers, along with three brothers and two sisters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-11) The family practiced [Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church "Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)

Kenenisa initially aspired to a career in medicine, education, or the civil service.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) He began to train seriously in running with the encouragement of a physical education teacher, while drawing inspiration from the success of Derartu Tulu and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) Kenenisa achieved his first medals at an international competition with second-place finishes in both the 3000 metres of the [1999 World Youth Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics") and the 5000 metres of the [2000 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Men's_200_metres "2000 World Junior Championships in Athletics – Men's 200 metres").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13) He won his first gold medal in the junior race of the [2001 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_men's_race "2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior men's race").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-14) His success in running enabled him to purchase a house and to help fund his siblings' educations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-15)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2001 – 2003: Early career")]

In August 2001, Kenenisa set a [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres")[world junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_junior_world_records_in_athletics "List of junior world records in athletics") by running 7:30.67 minutes in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"). The record lasted for three and a half years, being broken by [Augustine Choge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Choge "Augustine Choge") with a run of 7:28.78 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-16) In December 2000 and 2001 Kenenisa won the 15k roadrace Montferland Run in the Netherlands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) For five years in a row, from 2002 (at the age of 19) through 2006, he took both short (4 km) and long (12 km) races at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), a feat no other runner has accomplished even once.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-18) After the IAAF eliminated the short course race in 2007, Kenenisa won a final long course race in 2008, bringing his World Cross Country medal totals to 11 senior individual gold medals (6 long course, 5 short course), 1 senior silver medal (2001), 1 junior gold medal (2001), 2 team gold medals (2004, 2005), 3 team silver medals (2002, 2003, & 2008), and 1 team bronze medal (2006) for a grand total of 19 medals.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17)

Kenenisa became known for his ability to accelerate very quickly at the end of a long-distance race; in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") in June 2003, he chased after [Kenyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")[Abraham Chebii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chebii "Abraham Chebii") and won the race in 12:52.26.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) He has faced fellow Ethiopian, [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie"), twice in road competition, once in cross country, and six times on the track. Haile defeated Kenenisa on the track in the 2000 Nurnberg 5000 metres, the 2001 [Great Ethiopian Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ethiopian_Run "Great Ethiopian Run") 10 km, and the [Cross de l'Acier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_de_l'Acier "Cross de l'Acier") in December 2001, but lost to Kenenisa in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo") 2003 over 10,000 m (26:53 to 26:54), Rome 2003 over 5000 m (12:57 to 13:00), Paris [2003 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Championships in Athletics") over 10,000 m (26:49 to 26:50), [Athens 2004 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens_2004_Olympic_Games "Athens 2004 Olympic Games") (27:05 to 27:27), in the 10,000 m in the [Beijing 2008 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_2008_Olympic_Games "Beijing 2008 Olympic Games") (27:01 to 27:06), and in the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run")[half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") in September 2013 (60:09 to 60:41).

In 2004, Kenenisa broke the world records for the indoor 5000 m, outdoor 5000 m and outdoor 10,000 m (both in a timeframe of 9 days).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-19) He won the short and long course world cross country titles, leading Ethiopia to the senior men's team title. He also won a gold medal in the men's 10,000 metres and a silver medal in the men's 5000 metres in the 2004 Olympic Games in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-20)

On 4 January 2005, Kenenisa's fiancée, 18-year-old Alem Techale, died of an apparent heart attack while on a training run with him. Although it was initially stated that no [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") was performed, Alem's and Kenenisa's manager [Jos Hermens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos_Hermens "Jos Hermens") later said that an autopsy had revealed nothing conclusive about Techale's death. She was the [2003 World Youth Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Youth Championships in Athletics") in the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and in excellent physical condition.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-21)

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_-_Smiling.jpg)

Kenenisa competing in the 2006 Golden League.

He resumed racing on 29 January, and lost indoors over 3000 m to Ireland's [Alistair Cragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alistair_Cragg "Alistair Cragg") after sprinting towards the line with one and a half laps to go, while thinking that there was only half a lap left.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-22) A few weeks later he lost to fellow Ethiopian [Markos Geneti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markos_Geneti "Markos Geneti") over [two miles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_miles "Two miles").

In March, Kenenisa lined up to defend his long and short course titles at the [2005 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2005 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). He won on the short course despite a fast pace set by [Qatari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar "Qatar")[Saif Saaeed Shaheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saif_Saaeed_Shaheen "Saif Saaeed Shaheen"), and followed that win with a long course victory the next day over [Eritrean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea")[Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") and Kenyan rival [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").

On 8 August 2005, Kenenisa Bekele won the [gold medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the 10,000 m at the [2005 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2005 World Championships in Athletics") in Helsinki with a last [200 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/200_m "200 m") spurt.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-23) On 26 August 2005, Kenenisa set the [10,000 m world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_10000_metres_men "World record progression 10000 metres men") 26:17.53 at the 29th [Memorial Van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") meeting in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), slicing nearly three seconds off his previous world record 26:20.31, and running with 5000 m splits of 13:09 and 13:08 minutes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-24) The race saw 6 runners finishing in less than 27 minutes, with Sammy Wanjiru dipping in 26:41.75, a new world junior record. At the end of 2005 Kenenisa was voted the _[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ magazine athlete of the year for the second year in a row.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-25)

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_running.jpg)

Kenenisa leading the way at the 2007 Cross de Itálica.

When Kenenisa won the 3000 m at the [2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), he became the first athlete in history to be Olympic champion, world outdoor track champion, world indoor track champion, and world cross country champion.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-26) In 2006 he won five out of six [IAAF Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Golden_League "IAAF Golden League") events (5000 m) in the same season, which earned him a total of US$83,333.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-27)

On 17 February 2007, he broke the indoor world record over 2000 m in [Birmingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham "Birmingham"), with a time of 4:49.99. His spectacular final 300 m aided this time which would be considered excellent even outdoors.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-28) On 24 March 2007, however, his streak of 27 consecutive victories in cross country races (dating back to his last previous loss in December 2001) came to an end when after leading the race in the penultimate lap of the [2007 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2007 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") he succumbed to the very hot, humid conditions (which caused more than 1/6 of all competitors to drop out) and was passed by eventual winner [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") on the last lap before Kenenisa dropped out. This was greeted with cheers by the Kenyan crowds, an occurrence which has been frowned upon by the wider athletics community.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-29)

He recovered from that rare failure to take the 10,000-metre title at the [2007 IAAF World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Championships "2007 IAAF World Championships") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"), once again besting his compatriot [Sileshi Sihine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sileshi_Sihine "Sileshi Sihine"). During that race, he looked like he was going to be dropped several times over the last 800 metres, but recovered to overtake Sileshi with 150 metres to go and take his third straight world title.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-30)

### 2008: Beijing Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2008: Beijing Olympics")]

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_Berlin_2009.jpg)

Celebrating his gold medal victory at the 2009 World Championships.

In [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") on 30 March 2008, he won his sixth World Cross Country title (long course – 12k), breaking the three-way tie of 5 wins he had previously shared with [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat") and [John Ngugi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ngugi "John Ngugi"). With this win, Kenenisa laid sole claim to most decorated athlete in [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") history. He has won 6 long course (12k) individual gold medals, 5 short course (4k) gold medals, 1 junior championship (8k), and 4 team gold medals for a sum total of 16 gold medals. His overall medal count (both individual and team results) stands at 27 medals: 16 gold, 9 silver and 2 bronze.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-31)

On 17 August 2008 Kenenisa won gold in the 10,000m finals with a time of 27:01.17, setting a new [Olympic Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process. In a race in which 20 men broke the 28-minute barrier and four finished under his 2004 Olympic record of 27:05.10, he needed his renowned finishing kick to pull out the victory, running a 53.42-second final 400 metres (similar to the 53.02-second final 400-metre sprint he used to win the gold medal in Athens in 2004 over the same distance).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-BBC-32)

On 23 August 2008 Kenenisa bested his competitors and won the 5000-metre finals, shattering [Saïd Aouita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sa%C3%AFd_Aouita "Saïd Aouita")'s Olympic Record by almost eight seconds with a time of 12:57.82. The race was remarkable for his manner of doing most of the pacing himself before accelerating to a scintillating finish: his last 3000 metres only took 7:35.53, his final 2000 metres 4:56.97, last 1600 metres 3:57.01 (=3:58.4 final mile) and his final lap a punishing 53.87 seconds.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-33) By winning the 10,000/5000m double in the Beijing Olympics, Kenenisa joined another elite group of athletes: [Hannes Kolehmainen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannes_Kolehmainen "Hannes Kolehmainen") (1912), [Emil Zátopek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_Z%C3%A1topek "Emil Zátopek") (1952), [Vladimir Kuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Kuts "Vladimir Kuts") (1956), [Lasse Virén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasse_Vir%C3%A9n "Lasse Virén") (twice, in 1972 and 1976) and [Miruts Yifter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miruts_Yifter "Miruts Yifter") (1980).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-34)

### 2009: Berlin World Championships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2009: Berlin World Championships")]

Kenenisa Bekele won two gold medals at the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), held in Berlin. His double victories in 5000m (13:17.09) and 10,000m (26:46.31 – a World Championships Record) were unprecedented and by doing this became the first man to take both the long-distance track gold medals at the same World Championships.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-35) His talent combination of endurance and speed has made it nearly impossible to defeat Kenenisa when he is at full strength. During the 10,000m race in which he was running behind Eritrea's Zersenay Tadesse, the broadcaster declared "it is over, in fact it was over from the start" as the final lap began and Kenenisa turned an ostensibly close race into a blowout. The IAAF announcer concluded, "this man is probably the greatest distance runner we will ever see."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-36)

In spite of his unrivalled success in athletics, Kenenisa did not experience the mainstream appeal that others such as Haile Gebrselassie did. His quiet demeanour and aversion to interviews did not make him a highly marketable athlete in the [Western world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world"). Fellow [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics") holder [Usain Bolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usain_Bolt "Usain Bolt") stated that Kenenisa Bekele's achievements had not received the recognition that they deserved.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-37)

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Men%27s_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg/250px-Men%27s_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Men's_10000m_Final_-_2012_Olympics_-_4.jpg)

 Kenenisa pursuing the lead pack in the Men's 10,000 metres final event at the 2012 Summer Olympics.

Kenenisa made a disappointing start to 2010, finishing fourth in the [Edinburgh Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Cross_Country "Edinburgh Cross Country") in a race he was favored to win – a trio of Kenyan athletes ran him out of the contest over the final lap. He spent the entirety of the indoor and outdoor seasons out with a ruptured calf muscle.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-38)

### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics")]

Kenenisa Bekele finally returned to training after a knee injury in March 2011.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-39) Having not raced on the track since 2009, Kenenisa returned for the World Championships.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-40) He dropped out of the 10,000m with 10 laps remaining.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-41) Kenenisa decided not to run the 5000 m and[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-42) returned to the Diamond League at the [Ivo Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivo_Van_Damme_Memorial "Ivo Van Damme Memorial") in Brussels where he set the fastest time in the world for the 10,000 metres in 2011.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-44)

Kenenisa's 2012 season did not start well, as he was a lowly eleventh place at the Edinburgh Cross Country.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-45) In April, he appeared to have returned to form by winning the [Great Ireland Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Ireland_Run "Great Ireland Run") in a new personal best time for a 10 km road race of 27:49, improving the course record by 46 seconds.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-46)

In the [2012 London Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics")[10,000m race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") he ran within the leading group for the whole race, but could not keep up with the [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah")'s sprint in the last 150 metres and eventually finished fourth, with a time of 27:32.44, just 1.01 second outside the bronze medalist, his brother [Tariku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-47)

In his first race of 2013 he won the Great Ireland Run for a second time.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-48) Kenenisa then won the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 60:09, beating Mo Farah by just one second after making a move that Farah couldn't match with just less than 12 miles gone.

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg/250px-Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kenenisa_Bekele_2014_Paris_Marathon_t084500.jpg)

Kenenisa Bekele at the 2014 Paris Marathon

2014 - 2015
Kenenisa Bekele started his marathon career in the [2014 Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon#2014 "Paris Marathon") on 6 April 2014. His marathon debut was very successful as he bettered both the Paris course record and the debut marathon times of past legends Haile Gebrselassie, Paul Tergat and Samuel Wanjiru by running 2:05:04 to win.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-Letsrun.com-49) Kenenisa then went on to compete in the [2014 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Chicago_Marathon "2014 Chicago Marathon") on 12 October 2014. He finished fourth in 2:05:51, 1min 40s behind Kenya's [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-nbcsports.com-50) On 23 January 2015, Kenenisa took on the [Dubai Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_Marathon "Dubai Marathon"), where he had to retire from the race after 30 km.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-dubaimarathon.org-51) He was planned to compete in the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon") but had to withdraw due to a persistent injury to his right [Achilles tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles_tendon "Achilles tendon").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-runnersworld.com-52)

Following 11 months of injury, Kenenisa returned to racing at the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon"). Prior to the race he indicated he was only currently at 90% fitness. Kenenisa finished in 3rd place behind winner Eliud Kipchoge and runner-up [Stanley Biwott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Biwott "Stanley Biwott") in a time of 2:06:36. This performance was despite the fact he only returned to jogging in early 2016 following injury and had only completed 6 weeks of specific marathon training. He was also hampered in the race by missing his drinks at 5 separate stations, due to them being used by the designated pacemakers.

2016 - 2017
On 24 April, he placed third at the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon") with a time of two hours six minutes and 38 seconds. In September he won the [2016 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Berlin_Marathon "2016 Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03 which set a new personal best time for him at the [Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") distance and the second fastest marathon of all time.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-53) On 19 January 2017, attempting to break the world record, Kenenisa dropped out of the Dubai Marathon after the half way mark due to a fall at the beginning of the race.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-54) On 23 April 2017, Kenenisa finished second in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon"), finishing in 2:05:57, 9 seconds behind winner [Daniel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Wanjiru "Daniel Wanjiru").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-55)

Kenenisa's outstanding track career led to his involvement in a project to break the two-hour barrier for the marathon, though a number of factors undermined this effort.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-NYT_2hour-56)

2018 - 2019
Kenenisa ran the 2018 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") in April and came in sixth place with a time of 2:08:53.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-57) He also ran the Amsterdam marathon in October 2018 but dropped out due to injury with about 2 km to go.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-58) Kenenisa won the [2019 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Berlin_Marathon "2019 Berlin Marathon") in September in 2:01:41, the second fastest time ever at the time and just two seconds off of the world record set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") on the same course the previous year. After the run he stated that he still believes that he can break the world record.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-59)

2020 - 2021
Kenenisa won the London half marathon on 1 March 2020 in 60:22. He improved on the course record set by [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah") in 2019 by 1:18. [Chris Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Thompson_(runner) "Chris Thompson (runner)") came in second with 61:07, also within the former course record.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-61) Kenenisa returned to the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Berlin_Marathon "2021 Berlin Marathon") in September, where he placed third in 2:06:47. The race was won by his compatriot [Guye Adola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guye_Adola "Guye Adola") in 2:05:45, while Kenya's [Bethwel Yegon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethwel_Yegon "Bethwel Yegon") finished second.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-62) In November, he finished six at the [2021 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_New_York_City_Marathon "2021 New York City Marathon") with a time of 2:12:52.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2)

2022 - 2023
In September, he placed third at the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 1:01:01.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2) The next month, Kenenisa competed in the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"), finishing fifth in 2:05:53 to set a masters world record in age 40 group.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-63) In April, he took part in the London Marathon but withdrew from the race after 25k mark. Then, in October, he announced on Instagram that he had departed from the NN running team and transitioned his sponsorship from Nike to Anta, a Chinese sports brand. In December, Kenenisa took part in the Valencia Marathon. Although he fell behind the leading group before reaching the 15 km mark, he managed to finish fourth in a M40 Master World Record with a time of 2:04:19. This achievement solidifies him as the first athlete aged over 40 to complete a marathon in sub 2:05 clocking.

The 41-year-old Kenenisa competed in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_Marathon "2024 London Marathon") on 21 April 2024, where he finished second behind [Alexander Munyao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Mutiso_Munyao "Alexander Mutiso Munyao") breaking his own Masters record by 4 seconds running 2:04:15.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-64) Kenenisa was selected to represent Ethiopia in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"). At 41 years of age, it was his fourth Olympic appearance and first time competing at the event since the 2012 London Olympics.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-65) Kenenisa ended up finishing in 39th place with a time of 2:12:24[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-66)

On 18 November 2007, Kenenisa married [Ethiopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopians "Ethiopians") film actress Danawit Gebregziabher in Addis Ababa.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-67) Kenenisa has one younger brother, [Tariku Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele"), who is also an accomplished world-class distance runner.

The **10,000 metres** or the **10,000-metre run** is a common [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") track running event. The event is part of the [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") programme at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") and the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships"), and is common at championship-level events. The race consists of 25 laps around an Olympic-sized 400 m track. It is less commonly held at track and field meetings due to its duration. The 10,000-metre track race is usually distinguished from its [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") counterpart, the [10K run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run"), by referring to the distance in metres rather than kilometres.

The 10,000 metres is the longest standard track event, approximately equivalent to 6 miles 376 yards or 32,808 feet 5 inches.

[![Image 88](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10%2C000_m_world_record.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10,000_m_world_record.jpeg)

[Taisto Mäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki "Taisto Mäki") from [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") breaks the 30-minute barrier in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") on 17 September 1939.

Added to the Olympic programme in 1912, athletes from Finland, nicknamed the "[Flying Finns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Finn "Flying Finn")", dominated the event until the late 1940s. In the 1960s, African runners began to come to the fore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-1) In 1988, the women's competition debuted in the Olympic Games.

Official records are kept for outdoor 10,000-metre track events. The world record for men is held by [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") of [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") in 26:11.00, set in [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"), Spain on 7 October 2020. For women, the world record is held by [Beatrice Chebet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet "Beatrice Chebet") of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), in 28:54.14, set in Eugene, Oregon, on 25 May 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-2)

The 10,000 metres demands exceptional levels of aerobic endurance, and elite athletes typically train in excess of 160 km (100 miles) a week.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-3)

## 6 miles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=10,000_metres&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 6 miles")]

10,000 metres is the slightly longer metric derivative of the 6-mile (9,656.1-metre) run, an event common in countries when they were using the [imperial measurement system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_units "Imperial units"). 6 miles was used in the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the Commonwealth Games") until 1966 and was a [championship in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships") in non-Olympic years from 1953 to 1973. It is 24 laps around a 1⁄4-mile (402 m; 440 yd; 1,320 ft) track.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| [Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics") Half marathon |
| --- |
| [![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/BMW_Dallas_Marathon.jpg/330px-BMW_Dallas_Marathon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BMW_Dallas_Marathon.jpg) Half marathon runners in the 2024 [Dallas Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Marathon "Dallas Marathon") |
| [World records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics#World_records "List of world records in athletics") |
| Men | ![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Flag_of_Ethiopia.svg/40px-Flag_of_Ethiopia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha")(ETH) 56:51 (2026) |
| Women | **[Mx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_abbreviations#Circumstances_and_conditions "Athletics abbreviations")**: ![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Flag_of_Ethiopia.svg/40px-Flag_of_Ethiopia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Letesenbet Gidey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letesenbet_Gidey "Letesenbet Gidey")(ETH) 1:02:52 (2021) **[Wo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_abbreviations#Circumstances_and_conditions "Athletics abbreviations")**: ![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Flag_of_Kenya.svg/40px-Flag_of_Kenya.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Agnes Jebet Ngetich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Jebet_Ngetich "Agnes Jebet Ngetich")(KEN) 1:05:15 (2026) |

A **half marathon** is a [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") event of 21.0975 kilometres (c. 13 mi 192.5 yd)—half the distance of a [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-1) It is common for a half marathon event to be held concurrently with a marathon or a 5K race, using almost the same course with a late start, an early finish, or shortcuts.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-2)[_[circular reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Wikipedia\_and\_sources\_that\_mirror\_or\_use\_it "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] If finisher medals are awarded, the medal or ribbon may differ from those for the full marathon. The half marathon is also known by its [rounded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rounding "Rounding") distance: a _21K_, a _21.1K_, or _**13.1** miles_.

A [half marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon_world_record_progression "Half marathon world record progression") is officially recognised by [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-IAAF_men_record-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-IAAF_women_record-4) The men's world record time is 56:51, set by [Yomif Kejelcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomif_Kejelcha "Yomif Kejelcha") in 2026 in [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"). [Jacob Kiplimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo "Jacob Kiplimo") ran 56:42 in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona") in 2025, but this mark was not ratified by World Athletics due to his proximity to the lead car.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-5) The women's world record, in a mixed-gender race, is 1:02:52, set by [Letesenbet Gidey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letesenbet_Gidey "Letesenbet Gidey") of Ethiopia in October 2021 in [Valencia, Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"). The world record for the women's only race is 1:05:15, set by [Agnes Jebet Ngetich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Jebet_Ngetich "Agnes Jebet Ngetich") of Kenya in September 2026.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-6)

Participation in half marathons has grown steadily since 2003,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-nytimes-7) partly because it is a challenging distance, but does not require the same level of training that a marathon does.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-nytimes-7) In 2008, _Running USA_ reported that the half marathon was the fastest-growing type of race.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-nytimes-7)

Races close to the official half marathon distance of 21.0975 km (13.1094 mi) have taken place throughout the early 20th century, and athletes have also been timed at the midpoint of full [marathons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"). The [1946 Central American and Caribbean Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Central_American_and_Caribbean_Games "1946 Central American and Caribbean Games") in [Barranquilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barranquilla "Barranquilla"), Colombia featured a road race that is listed at exactly the modern half marathon distance, referred to as the "Carrera Centroamericana y del Caribe: (21 kms. 97,5 metros)".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-8) The [1952 South American Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_South_American_Championships_in_Athletics "1952 South American Championships in Athletics") in [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), Argentina featured a road race that was 21.097km, referred to as "la media maratón" ('the half marathon') by the Chilean newspaper _La Nación._[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-9)

The earliest half marathon recognised by the [ARRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Road_Racing_Statisticians "Association of Road Racing Statisticians") is the 1960 [Romford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romford "Romford") Half Marathon in England, though it was short of the full half marathon distance.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-10) The earliest half marathon recognised by [World Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics") is the 1965 [Feckleton Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freckleton_Half_Marathon "Freckleton Half Marathon") in England. The event grew in popularity, leading to the eventual establishment of the [World Athletics Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships "World Athletics Road Running Championships") in 1992, originally titled the IAAF World Half Marathon Championships.

*   Updated 23 August 2026.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-12)

The [Chicago Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Half_Marathon "Chicago Half Marathon") is a [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") tune-up on [Lake Shore Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Shore_Drive "Lake Shore Drive") in the [South Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side_(Chicago) "South Side (Chicago)") of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago").

[![Image 72](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Bristol_Half_Marathon.jpg/330px-Bristol_Half_Marathon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bristol_Half_Marathon.jpg)

Runners taking part in the [Bristol Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Half_Marathon "Bristol Half Marathon")

This table lists the best half marathon performances per year since 1970, as recorded by the [ARRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Road_Racing_Statisticians "Association of Road Racing Statisticians").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-ARRSRankingsHalf-60)

The largest half marathon ever held was [Broloppet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broloppet "Broloppet") (the Bridge race) between [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen") in Denmark and [Malmö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malm%C3%B6 "Malmö") in Sweden with 79,719 finishers, held in connection with the [Øresund Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund_Bridge "Øresund Bridge") inauguration in 2000.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon#cite_note-64)
